justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely somewhere in the mid-to-upper 370s range for a broad equity index or commodity. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price with only a small drift adjustment, since markets tend to mean-revert over very short windows and overnight gaps rarely move prices dramatically without a clear catalyst. For the one-week estimate, I allowed for slightly more drift, reflecting the general long-run upward bias in risk assets while acknowledging that a week is long enough for sentiment shifts to matter. The one-month estimate pushed a bit higher still, consistent with a baseline assumption of modest positive expected returns, though the incremental drift beyond the one-week horizon is small relative to the uncertainty added.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how volatility compounds over time. At one day, historical daily moves of roughly 1–2% in either direction constrain the plausible range fairly tightly. Over one week, roughly five trading days of compounding uncertainty widens the band considerably, and at one month the interval expands further to account for the possibility of a sustained trend in either direction. I also factored in that macro data releases, central bank communications, and geopolitical developments tend to cluster unpredictably, meaning the distribution of outcomes has heavier tails than a simple Gaussian model would suggest — hence intervals that widen somewhat more aggressively than a pure square-root-of-time scaling would imply.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a surprise policy shift from a major central bank, an unexpected inflation print that significantly changes rate expectations, or a geopolitical shock such as an escalation in an ongoing conflict or a sudden trade policy announcement. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season or a resolution of a known geopolitical risk could drive prices above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for a narrative shift to take hold. These tail risks are precisely why the one-month interval is wide enough to encompass roughly a 10–15% swing from the point estimate while still leaving meaningful probability mass outside those bounds.
